_about: THE EMPEROR'S DIARY (EN, @EmperorsDiary-en) — English adaptation of the latest Korean longform cine_ep01 '나에게 뒤통수 친 사람을 이기는 3가지 방법 | 명상록' (YouTube IJ7NXFssjys, 9:55, 2026-11-10 19:34 KST). Source: scripts/side/ed_long/cine_ep01.py (+ cine01.py). Keys of 'lines' are the indices of cine_ep01.L (same scene/clip order and timing); 'insert' keys are cine_ep01.NEWV. Voices: N = narrator, M = emperor (Marcus), V = general Verus, C = Cassius. Meditations quotes: George Long (1862, public domain), lightly modernized. Status 2026-11-11: Phase 1 (script + voice test). Not rendered.

0: !What's the perfect revenge on someone who betrayed you?
1: Two thousand years ago, a man was handed a box.
2: Inside were the names of everyone who betrayed him.
3: All he had to do was open it.
4: Instead, he threw it into the fire.
7: Ten years earlier, one general's name was spreading along Rome's eastern frontier.
8: In the war with Parthia, he drove all the way to the enemy's capital.
11: The emperor trusted him. He gave him the entire East.
12: The armies, the provinces, even the power to wage war.
13: Spring, 175 AD. The emperor was far away, on the Danube frontier.
14: At fifty-four, he had spent winter after winter in a tent.
15: And that year, the emperor collapsed.
16: The illness was serious, and the rumors moved faster than he could.
17: His heir, his son Commodus, was only thirteen.
18: At his side, the empress Faustina was afraid.
19: If her husband died, what would happen to their boy?
20: One account says she wrote to Cassius in secret.
21: If the emperor dies, she asked, take the empire.
22: Remember that letter. No one knows the truth.
25: In April 175, Cassius stood before his army and declared himself emperor.
26: The emperor is dead. Rome follows me now.
27: Syria and Egypt went over to him.
28: But a few days later, different news arrived.
30: He could have turned back. He could have called it a mistake.
32: Only then did the news reach the emperor on the Danube.
33: It was brought by Martius Verus, governor of Cappadocia.
34: In that letter was the name of the man he trusted most.
35: Him? Why... why him, of all people?
36: At first, the emperor kept the news to himself.
37: But the rumor spread from tent to tent.
39: He gathered his men. Everyone expected a speech full of rage.
40: Soldiers. I have not come here to rage.
41: I have come to grieve my fate.
42: The friend I held dearest has plotted against me.
43: From this war, I want only one thing.
44: To forgive the man who wronged me.
45: To remain a friend to the one who broke our friendship.
47: By every record, he never cursed him.
48: The only word he used for him was 'ungrateful.'
49: In the Meditations, there is this line.
50: Above all, when you blame someone as faithless or ungrateful, turn to yourself.
51: Trusting him had been his own choice.
52: The emperor rushed to end the war in the north.
53: Barbarian chiefs offered to send troops to help him.
54: What happens between Romans is not for your eyes.
55: Then he led his army east.
56: To meet Cassius alive, and to forgive him.
59: A centurion named Antonius rode up to Cassius.
60: The blade caught his neck. The wound was not fatal.
61: The horse carried on, and another officer finished it.
63: That was how long he was emperor.
64: His head was on its way to the emperor.
65: Bury it. I will not look.
66: He ordered it buried before it ever reached him.
67: I wanted to meet him alive. Now there is no one left to forgive.
69: The best way to avenge yourself is not to become like the one who wronged you.
70: Some time later, a chest arrived before the emperor.
72: Senators, generals, governors. Everyone who helped him. It's all in here.
74: No. You should see them first.
75: If I read these... who will I see tomorrow?
77: No. From tomorrow, I would see a traitor in every face.
79: Caesar, these men wanted you dead.
80: And so I should become like them?
82: Another account says Verus burned them for him.
83: What is certain is this: those names survive nowhere.
84: The Senate demanded the conspirators be punished.
85: Let no senator's blood be shed in my reign.
87: Cassius's son was killed. Others were exiled.
89: Whether he ever suspected her, the records don't say.
90: But in his list of things he thanked the gods for, he wrote this.
91: That I had such a wife, so loving, and so sincere.
94: A business partner. A brother. An old friend.
95: Imagine the messages that show exactly what they said about you
96: were in your hand tonight. Would you open them?
97: Open them, and you get the names. But you carry those names for the rest of your life.
98: Three ways to beat someone who betrayed you.
99: One. Don't curse them. Those words only dirty your own mouth.
100: Two. Don't stand and watch their downfall.
101: Three. Don't open what you don't need to know.

n1: Born in Syria, he was a general known for discipline harsh enough to frighten his own men.
n2: When Egypt, Rome's breadbasket, fell to him, the Senate declared Cassius a public enemy.
n3: Half the empire could become his enemy overnight.
n4: He called his thirteen-year-old son to his side and named him heir.
n5: Afterward, the emperor toured the East and showed mercy to the cities that had joined the revolt.
